overview: The atlas colors an Andean polygon as “Uru” from approximately 1492 to 1500, but its imported summary describes a Kerala boat. That namesake is suppressed. The polygon is an editorial layer, not a surveyed frontier, unified state, or title map. Its 1492 shape overlaps twenty-three other labels and assigns tested places to multiple owners. Peru's Indigenous Peoples Database describes living Uro people around Lake Titicaca, fishing, bird hunting, totora work, family islands, tourism, language loss, and multilingual history. That profile illuminates one Peruvian context; it does not prove that every place inside the atlas color shared one government, language, livelihood, or identity. Sections distinguish other communities and uses of the name through dated sources. Later sections use carefully dated evidence, name its limits, and avoid projecting modern sources into 1492. Eight one-year bands organize uncertainty rather than invent annual events. The exact label ends at a software seam in 1500. The card treats that as a map transition, while living Uro communities and their knowledge continue beyond it.

periods.title: An approximate atlas layer appears
periods.summary: The exact id appears once, in the 1492 border file, as one approximate polygon with a 1500 endpoint. The index supplies no capital, ruler, law, founding event, or surveyed frontier. This first band therefore dates the database layer, while rejecting its imported Kerala boat summary and default state classification.

periods.title: Fishing evidence crosses many centuries
periods.summary: No source identifies a special event in 1493. Scholarship on fishing under Inca rule instead combines archaeological and ethnohistorical evidence about specialization, administration, and tribute around Lake Titicaca. It supplies regional context for the atlas interval, but cannot identify one fisher, settlement, or Uru political boundary in this editorial year.

periods.title: Archaeology warns against a frozen portrait
periods.summary: Nothing securely singles out 1494. Zooarchaeological study of faunal remains from 367 flotation samples at five Titicaca Basin sites spans roughly 1500 BCE to 1100 CE and finds fishing changed with environment and society. The long sequence proves neither a timeless lake economy nor the ethnicity of every fisher near the later atlas polygon.

periods.title: Official history offers cautious synthesis
periods.summary: No annual event is assigned to 1495. Peru's Indigenous Peoples Database summarizes traditions of Inca incorporation and tribute in fish and straw containers, then turns to colonial reports from the 1570s. Useful as synthesis, it cannot transform later accounts into a dated diary or exact boundary for this year.

periods.title: A name was also an administrative category
periods.summary: No surviving register securely describes 1496. Catherine Julien shows that later colonial officials used an Uru tribute category with lower assessments, occupations, language labels, and social judgments that did not map neatly onto one people. Her analysis helps interpret documents after conquest, while refusing a simple ethnic back-projection.

periods.title: The earliest detailed survey comes later
periods.summary: The packet has no contemporary record for 1497. Garci Diez de San Miguel's 1567 Chucuito visitation preserves questions, testimony, labor, tribute, and administrative observations decades after conquest. It is invaluable primary evidence, but its colonial purpose and later date prevent treating every listed Uru household as a 1497 census.

periods.title: Speech survives unevenly in later records
periods.summary: No securely dated Uru manuscript survives from 1498. Linguistic documentation begins centuries later and distinguishes Ch'imu, Irohito or Uchumataqu, Chipaya, and related materials with different histories. These records recover words and structures, yet they do not reveal a standardized alphabet, one uniform language, or an inscription from the atlas interval.

periods.title: A repaint is not a disappearance
periods.summary: The exact id vanishes in the 1500 snapshot, where every tested point inside its former shape receives the broad Inca Empire label. Three sampled ownership sets change again by 1530. Those are atlas edits, not evidence of collective death, one conquest in 1500, or the end of Uru and Uro communities.

sections.title: Read the atlas before trusting the color

items.text: The index names Uru and dates it approximately 1492 to 1500. Coverage calls it a state, while the imported summary and source lead describe a Kerala dhow. Those mismatched fields are catalog history, not evidence. This card suppresses the boat namesake and reclassifies the exact id as an approximate cultural layer.

Decoded geometry is one Polygon with one ring, 38 stored positions, and 37 unique positions. Its bounding box runs from about 71.07 to 64.09 degrees west and 23.72 to 15.18 degrees south. Those numbers fingerprint the file; they do not turn its angular outline into a historical survey.

Exact polygon tests find positive-area overlap with twenty-three atlas labels, including Aymara, Quechua, Chango, Kolla, Charka, Chichas, Kallawaya, and several others. Only the Chango shape shares a direct arc. One color therefore cannot make the map's overlapping editorial layers behave like a tidy passport office.

Puno and Uros Chulluni sit simultaneously in Quechua, Aymara, and Uru layers. Desaguadero and Irohito also fall within Aymara, Pakajaqi, and Uru; Oruro lies in Aymara, Sura, and Uru. These reproducible probes expose overlapping map categories, not three governments stamping the same travel document.

The exact feature is absent in checked snapshots for 1400, 1500, and 1530. Seventeen representative points change at both its 1492 appearance and its 1500 removal; three change again by 1530. The sequence measures cartographic repainting. It cannot date a migration, defeat, merger, extinction, or change in self-identification.

sections.title: Keep different Uru and Uro histories visible

items.text: Peru's official profile describes the living Uro people of Lake Titicaca, especially communities in Puno, and notes fishing, bird hunting, totora work, tourism, and family islands. It also records language loss and multilingual history. This evidence supports Peruvian Uro continuity, not ownership of the entire atlas polygon.

The DOBES documentation project separates Chipaya and Ayparavi speakers, Irohito near Lake Titicaca, Lake Poopó communities, and Puno's floating-island Uro. Their languages, livelihoods, and recent histories differ. Grouping them for comparative research is useful; collapsing them into one timeless society would erase precisely what the project records.

A population-genetics study distinguishes several meanings of Uru and describes sampled communities, language shifts, multilingualism, and informed consent. Genetic patterns can address population history under stated models. They cannot certify cultural authenticity, decide who belongs to a community, or make every historically labeled Uru person biologically interchangeable.

Michael Kent's ethnography examines how Uro people represent themselves amid tourism, territorial politics, oral history, scholarship, and arguments about ancestry. Identity is lived and negotiated, not a laboratory score. DNA may inform one historical question, but it cannot serve as a membership card or overrule community self-identification.

Nathan Wachtel traces hostile colonial and scholarly stereotypes that portrayed aquatic Uru populations as less than fully human. Those descriptions reveal power and prejudice in the sources, not neutral anthropology. A careful card can discuss an aquatic axis and imposed categories without repeating old insults as if they were reliable character sketches.

sections.title: Fish, gather, eat, and know the water

items.text: Archaeological fish remains from five Titicaca Basin sites cover about 2,600 years and show that fishing intensity varied with environmental and social change. This deep record makes fish historically important without making one recipe eternal. The samples end centuries before 1492 and do not assign each fisher a later ethnic label.

An Oxford Handbook chapter treats Titicaca fishing under Inca rule through archaeology and ethnohistory, including specialization, administration, and tribute. That is stronger than assuming everyone fished identically. It still provides regional context rather than a household diary, and it does not convert the atlas's Uru shape into an Inca tax district.

Community researchers record group fishing around Puno with nets, boats, shared labor, and knowledge of places and conditions. Their 2019 testimonies show skill practiced and explained by people. They are excellent evidence for recent teaching and cooperation, while remaining centuries too late to script a particular 1492 fishing trip.

The same community study describes gathering bird eggs in appropriate seasons and serving lake foods at family occasions, including marriage-related meals. Seasonality and celebration link ecology with social life. These reported practices are dated modern testimony, not permission to invent every fifteenth-century wedding menu, seating plan, or egg basket.

Research around Lake Titicaca describes modern communal fishing territories shaped by local ecology and social control. It demonstrates that water can be organized through community rules even when borders look fluid from shore. Those contemporary territories are not a cadastral key for decoding the much larger and earlier 1492 atlas polygon.

sections.title: Build with totora and maintain what floats

items.text: Peru's heritage resolution explains that floating islands begin with buoyant q'illi root blocks cut and joined, then covered by crisscrossed layers of totora. The documented technique combines plant knowledge, cutting, binding, placement, and teamwork. This is detailed modern heritage evidence, not a blueprint recovered from a 1492 workshop.

Fresh totora must be added as lower layers decay, and islands are anchored and repaired rather than simply launched and forgotten. Houses and working surfaces depend on continued maintenance. Floating does not mean effortless: the island is closer to a very large garden chore than a magic carpet with reeds.

The resolution also describes selecting and drying reeds, building boats, using tools, and fitting sails. These linked skills turn wetland plants into transport and architecture. The record supports engineering achievement among today's Uro communities; it does not prove that every vessel, sail, or tool had identical form across the fifteenth-century polygon.

Peru's official profile says newer floating islands commonly hold one or two families and describes totora as central to homes, handicrafts, boats, and tourism. The small household scale makes daily maintenance social and practical. It documents present Puno life, not one universal residence pattern for all historical Uru groups.

Community accounts describe children learning fishing, hunting, and totora-related water work by accompanying parents; one father made a small balsa for his child. These concrete scenes show intergenerational teaching and care. They do not establish one uniform boat-making lesson, nor do the 2019 testimonies date that learning to 1492.

sections.title: Meet families, neighbors, workers, and visitors

items.text: Kent describes islands that may merge, divide, or move as households and relationships change. Territorial practice can be flexible even when government maps demand fixed boundaries. This modern ethnography helps explain why family and community cannot be reduced to neat polygons, but it does not reconstruct an island roster for 1492.

The official Uros Chulluni locality record dates state recognition to 1975 and land title to 1994. It also supplies 2007 population, age, Indigenous-language, and school data. These are useful modern benchmarks for one named community, not the founding date of Uro identity or a census of the atlas layer.

Households negotiate relations with neighboring islands, tourism operators, government agencies, and wider communities; Kent shows that territorial claims shift with these connections. Social life is therefore political as well as domestic. The study concerns recent Puno conditions and should not be turned into a timeless family constitution for every Uru group.

DOBES reports tourism, fishing, bird hunting, craft work, and children's meetings among the distinct communities it documented. These activities reveal modern households balancing lake knowledge with cash income and organized teaching. Their mix differs by place, so no single job list can stand for Puno, Irohito, Poopó, and Chipaya alike.

The DOBES project recorded interviews with community participants, including native-speaker conversations, water knowledge, music, and local histories, while also teaching an alphabet in some settings. Its archive is collaborative but selective. A recorded interview preserves particular voices; it does not authorize one composite speaker for all Uru-Chipaya communities.

sections.title: Hear languages and read one later sample

items.text: Uru-Chipaya documentation distinguishes Chipaya, Irohito or Uchumataqu, Ch'imu, and other recorded material, with substantial Aymara contact and very different vitality. Only Chipaya remained robust in the project's account. These related varieties must not be treated as one unchanged tongue spoken uniformly across the atlas polygon in 1498.

Written sample: hŭắsē, meaning “water.” Hannß's comparative vocabulary attributes this exact Ch'imu form to Walter Lehmann's 1929 Puno material. It is a collector-specific Latin transcription preserved in a modern scholarly database, not standardized spelling, not proof of one pan-Uru form, and certainly not a surviving 1492 manuscript.

Hannß explains that the vocabulary compares sources from 1894 to 2005 and deliberately preserves their differing transcription systems. Its focus includes Irohito or Ancoaqui material, not a reconstructed medieval standard. Readers can compare forms responsibly only by keeping collector, place, date, and notation attached to each spelling.

Peru's language registry distinguishes Uru-Chipaya varieties and reports roughly three hundred Ch'imu words gathered in Puno in 1929. It classifies Peruvian Uro as extinct while documenting recovery efforts. “Extinct” here describes intergenerational language transmission, not the people, their identity, or their continuing community life.

A Ministry of Culture course taught 88 pupils and 12 teachers greetings, numbers, colors, family terms, plants, birds, fish, conversation, poetry, and songs. Planned adult and intermediate stages extend that work. This is modern revitalization through schools and community participation, not evidence for a standardized classroom in 1492.

sections.title: Treat health and medicine as dated evidence

items.text: Community researchers report plant and animal remedies, household postpartum care, offerings in a Quta mama ritual, visits from doctors and nurses, and a health post established in 2010. These dated accounts document care without establishing clinical efficacy or giving medical instructions. They cannot be copied into a 1492 medicine chest.

A university thesis sampled water from five named floating islands between May and July 2016, measuring microbial, physical, and chemical qualities relevant to drinking. This provides a dated study design and local evidence. It cannot describe every island, every season, or the water encountered by people five centuries earlier.

Peru's Ministry of Culture documented COVID-19 vaccination on the floating islands through coordination among health workers, community authorities, and cultural personnel. Uro participants received information and materials in Aymara and Quechua. The event shows modern public health outreach; it says nothing about fifteenth-century epidemics, immunity, clinics, or language use.

A housing-ministry assessment describes a Cappi Los Uros project serving 256 residents and 109 students with water treatment and twenty floating composting-sanitation modules. The numbers document planned modern infrastructure. They should not be generalized to all Uros Chulluni islands or mistaken for toilets available during the atlas interval.

No reviewed source securely names a remedy, healer, birth practice, epidemic, or care institution for the atlas years 1492 to 1500. Later colonial and community records cannot fill that silence automatically. The honest result is a dated evidence gap, not a diagnosis and not an invitation to invent an ancient hospital.

sections.title: Ask about toilets, waste, and safe water

items.text: The atlas and reviewed fifteenth-century evidence identify no Uru toilet, latrine, sewer, refuse pit, washing rule, or wastewater system. Silence is not permission to invent a floating throne, and it does not prove neglect. Sanitation claims below are modern, named projects whose dates and service areas remain attached.

At Cappi Los Uros, the assessed system combines water treatment with twenty floating composting-sanitation modules. The official document identifies one project and its intended population. It does not report results for every household or island, and it cannot support a toilet design or sanitation routine for the atlas interval.

EMSAPUNO's 2024 annual report marks the Uros Chulluni potable-water project “Culminado” while recording 91.05 percent physical progress, financing, schedule, and its access goal. Those fields document the utility's completed-project status. They do not by themselves establish universal household connections, continuous safe supply, or water quality.

Puno's municipality reported transferring 750,000 soles toward completing the potable-water project, with municipal, utility, and Uros Chulluni authorities participating. The payment shows cooperation and an unfinished need at that date. It does not by itself certify water safety, continuous supply, completed connections, or service across all floating islands.

OEFA joined lake and water authorities to monitor water quality near the Uros islands with municipal and community leaders present. Monitoring creates evidence; it is not automatically a clean-water verdict. The field report should be read with later laboratory results, and its modern measurements cannot be back-projected to 1492.

sections.title: Read colonial records without inheriting their bias

items.text: Julien shows that “Uru” in tribute records could function as an administrative category tied to lower assessments, occupations, mobility, and social rank. It did not always equal language or self-identified peoplehood. Counting category entries is therefore not the same as mapping a single ethnic nation backward onto 1492.

Colonial descriptions often linked Uru status with fishing, hunting water birds, reed work, poverty, and supposed primitiveness. Julien separates fiscal evidence from stereotype and tracks category changes. Livelihood clues can be historically valuable, but insults and administrative shortcuts reveal colonial interests as much as they reveal the people described.

Garci Diez de San Miguel's visitation records questions and testimony about households, resources, service, and tribute in Chucuito. As a primary document, it preserves voices through an official interrogation designed for administration. Every answer therefore needs context: colonial paperwork can be detailed without being neutral, complete, or contemporary with 1492.

The visitation's later paleographic edition lets readers inspect a sixteenth-century survey rather than rely only on summary. Yet spelling, translation, questioning, and fiscal categories mediate what survives. It cannot resolve every speaker's identity or extend one Chucuito observation across Puno, Irohito, Poopó, Chipaya, and the full atlas polygon.

Wachtel's open study follows aquatic populations, mobility, tribute, language, and social categories across sixteenth- and seventeenth-century records. It treats the “Uru problem” as a problem of sources and historical classification. That approach helps expose contradictions; its broad axis still should not become one bounded, homogeneous nation.

Peru's Law 30729 declares protection of the Uros people and Uros Chulluni, especially cultural and language recovery, to be of national interest and public necessity. The law is a modern state commitment responding to living communities. It neither creates Uro identity in 2018 nor authenticates the atlas polygon's boundaries.

The National Archive identifies the 23 October 1975 resolution recognizing Uros Chulluni and reports a community effort to protect that document as cultural heritage. It also notes more than one hundred inhabited floating islands today. Administrative recognition is historically important, while community life and identity plainly precede the paper.

Rodolfo Cerrón-Palomino's PUCP study reconstructs the Uro of Puno through linguistic records and an aquatic axis from Titicaca toward Coipasa, while identifying Chipaya as the related surviving language. This scholarly achievement recovers fragile evidence. It does not merge every community or turn linguistic relationship into one political boundary.

In a PUCP interview, Cerrón-Palomino explains how Lehmann's 1929 material helped recover Puno Uro vocabulary, discusses language replacement and multilingualism, and contrasts Peruvian extinction with Chipaya transmission. The distinction matters: a language can stop being transmitted while people, memories, names, and cultural projects continue.

Bolivia's IPELC reports review of a standardized Spanish to Uru-Chipaya dictionary, teaching booklet, and related educational materials by the Uru language and culture institute. Community-facing texts make revitalization practical for learners. This achievement belongs to present Bolivian institutions and must not be mislabeled as Peruvian Ch'imu revival or 1492 writing.

ending.text: The exact Uru polygon disappears when the atlas switches from its 1492 snapshot to 1500, but no cited source records an extinction, evacuation, surrender, or political collapse in that year. Every tested point inside the former shape is repainted as Inca Empire, and three sampled ownership sets change again by 1530. These file changes identify a software seam, not a people's ending. In 2018, Peru's president and Ministry of Culture recognized the Uros as an Indigenous people. Community authorities presented themselves as Qhas Qut Suñis, people of the lake, while the announcement emphasized cultural protection, language recovery, and a wastewater plan. Those are modern actions involving living people. They do not validate the imported polygon as a fifteenth-century state or date a collective ending in 1500. The conclusion therefore stays within the evidence: the database feature stops, while officially recognized Peruvian Uro people, community authorities, language-recovery work, and lake-linked cultural traditions remain documented centuries later. Other Uru or Uro communities have their own evidence and dates elsewhere in the card; this Peruvian recognition source is not used to speak for them.
